course_description: Study of Asian American literature and culture, with a focus on a specific topic, theme, movement, or genre. Students develop a deeper understanding of a specific topic and analyze literature and culture in relation to Asian American history and politics.
course_notes: This course will explore the rich history of memoir, life-writing, and creative nonfiction in Asian American literature and culture. We will read a several different kinds of memoir: coming-of-age stories, memorials, family histories, poetry, writing that combines fact and fiction or realism and fantasy, travel writing, graphic narrative, longform journalism, documentary film. Themes we will encounter include the immigrant¿s experience of loss and gain; entanglements and estrangements between generations; the playfulness and complexity of bilingual writing; the difficulty of retrieving the past; the way that secrets shape and structure narrative; the issue of gender in family history; the relative status and power of ¿tradition¿ and ¿originality¿; claiming voice and breaking silence; humor and parody as tools to fight against discrimination and prejudice; the role of food in memory. Requirements: Two papers, one of which will allow creative as well as academic options. Two bluebook tests, active and consistent participation in class discussions and exercises. And a substantial amount of reading and viewing outside of class. Texts: (tentative) books and stories by Maxine Hong Kingston, Cathy Park Hong, Hua Hsu, Michelle Zauner, Ocean Vuong, Andrew Pham, Abraham Verghese, Kay Sohini, Lee Ann Roripaugh, Simu Liu, Chantha Nguon, Kimiko Hahn, Micheal Ondaatje, Film and Television: First Person Plural, Forbidden City, USA.
